result: Force Profile Analysis (FPA) is a method that uses arrest peptides (APs) as force sensors to measure pulling forces on nascent chains during translation. APs bind in the ribosome exit tunnel and pause translation proportionally to the force exerted, with the fraction of full-length protein (fFL) serving as a proxy for force. This method can achieve single-residue resolution and has been previously used to study cotranslational folding and membrane integration.
evaluation: Claims C1-C7 describe the FPA methodology with appropriate citations to prior work. The method is well-established in the literature (C1-C6 cite supporting references), and the technical details about resolution (C7) are explicitly stated. These are methodological claims supported by prior publications.

result: EmrE is a dual-topology protein where monomers integrate in a 50-50 mixture of Nin-Cin and Nout-Cout topologies and assemble into antiparallel dimers. TMH1 is only marginally hydrophobic due to the functionally important E14 residue and does not become firmly embedded in the membrane until dimerization.
evaluation: Claims C8, C9, C12, and C13 describe established properties of EmrE with appropriate citations to prior work (Chen et al., 2007; Rapp et al., 2007; Seurig et al., 2019). These are background claims about the protein being studied.

result: The E14L mutation in EmrE(Cout) causes a clear peak to appear at Nstart ≈ 50 residues in the force profile, while E14A yields an intermediate fFL value, and E14D and E14Q mutations show the same fFL as wild-type EmrE(Cout) at N = 55.
evaluation: Claims C14-C16 describe experimental results with explicit reference to Figure 2b,c showing the data. The mutations systematically probe the role of E14 hydrophobicity, and the results are internally consistent with the hypothesis that TMH1 hydrophobicity affects force profile peaks.

result: Mutations in E14 of EmrE(Cout) TMH1 have long-range, position-dependent effects on the pulling forces generated by downstream TMHs during membrane integration. A negatively charged residue (D or E) at position 14 specifically reduces pulling force at N = 85 (during TMH2 integration), while mutations affect forces at N = 115 (TMH3) and N = 130 (TMH4). This implies TMH1 remains near the translocon and E14 makes specific interactions with residues in the TMH2-TMH4 region during integration.
evaluation: Claims C17-C25 describe a systematic set of mutation experiments with statistical significance testing (Figure 2c, p < 0.05-0.001) showing position-dependent effects. The data support the inference that TMH1 remains near the translocon during downstream TMH integration (C24-C25), though the specific molecular interactions remain to be determined. The negative control at N = 105 strengthens the conclusion.

result: EmrE(Cout) TMHs generate peaks in the force profile when their N-terminal ends are ~45 residues from the PTC (peaks III and IV at Nstart ≈ 102 and 132 residues, respectively) and cease generating force when their C-terminal ends are ~45 residues from the PTC, indicating full integration at this point.
evaluation: Claims C26-C29 describe consistent observations across multiple TMHs with data shown in Figures 2d,e. The ~45 residue distance is consistent with prior work (C10-C11) and represents a key finding about the spatial relationship between the PTC and the translocon. The use of the stronger SecM(Ec-sup1) AP to resolve peak IV (C27) demonstrates methodological rigor.

result: The ~60 residue N-terminal domain (NTD) of GlpG folds inside the ribosome exit tunnel when its C-terminal end is 25-30 residues from the PTC, well before membrane domain synthesis begins. This was verified by in vitro FPA and a destabilizing F16E mutation that reduces fFL values for peak I both in vivo and in vitro. The NTD has sufficient time to equilibrate between folded and unfolded states given its predicted ms folding time and the ~100 ms/codon elongation rate.
evaluation: Claims C31-C37 describe a well-controlled experiment with multiple lines of evidence: in vivo FP, in vitro FP, and destabilizing mutation (Figure 3b,c). The kinetic argument (C33-C35) is supported by appropriate citations. This represents a clear demonstration of cotranslational folding in the exit tunnel before membrane integration.

result: Peak III in the GlpG force profile is composed of three subpeaks (III-a, III-b, III-c) revealed by higher-resolution FPA. Subpeak III-a (Nstart = 182) corresponds to a periplasmic surface helix, III-b (Nstart ≈ 190) to TMH2 N-terminus reaching the translocon, and III-c (N ≈ 197-204) to insertion of the most hydrophobic part of TMH2. The Y138F139L143→NNN mutation strongly reduces peak III-a amplitude and shifts peak III-c, indicating the periplasmic surface helix engages in hydrophobic interactions during translocon passage and adds to the force generated by TMH2 integration.
evaluation: Claims C42-C50 describe high-resolution FPA with three different APs (SecM(Ec), SecM(Ec-Ms), SecM(Ec-Sup1)) revealing substructure in peak III (Figure 3d,f). The triple mutation experiment provides strong support for the role of the periplasmic surface helix. The interpretation is consistent with the sliding model (C49 cites Cymer et al., 2015b).

result: Integration of GlpG TMH3 is delayed, commencing only when its N-terminal end is ~52 residues from the PTC (rather than the typical ~45 residues), possibly due to tight spacing between TMH2 and TMH3.
evaluation: Claim C40 describes an observation (delayed integration), but C41 offers only a speculative explanation without experimental validation. While the observation is supported by data, the mechanistic explanation remains uncertain and would require additional experiments to confirm.

result: Peak VI-a in the GlpG force profile likely reflects membrane integration of a hydrophobic, membrane-associated cytoplasmic segment upstream of TMH5.
evaluation: Claim C39 is presented as a likely interpretation but lacks direct experimental validation (e.g., mutations in this segment). The claim is speculative and would benefit from mutagenesis experiments similar to those performed for the periplasmic surface helix.

result: BtuC force profile analysis identified 11 peaks, one more than the 10 TMHs. Systematic mutagenesis of hydrophobic residues 40-50 residues from the PTC caused significant drops in fFL (p < 0.01) for most constructs, allowing assignment of peaks I-V and VIII-XI to TMHs 1-5 and 7-10, respectively. Peaks VIII and IX appear to represent concerted integration of closely spaced TMH7 and TMH8.
evaluation: Claims C52-C55 describe systematic mutagenesis experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) with statistical testing. The approach is rigorous and the peak assignments are supported by the mutation data. The interpretation of overlapping peaks VIII/IX (C55) is reasonable given the close spacing of TMH7 and TMH8.

result: BtuC peak II (TMH2) is shifted to unexpectedly high Nstart values compared to isolated TMH2, which shows Nstart at the expected ~45 residues from PTC. Three upstream Arg residues delay TMH2 integration by ~10 residues; replacing these with Gln residues restores the expected integration timing. This indicates upstream positively charged residues delay membrane integration of Nout-oriented TMH2.
evaluation: Claims C56-C64 describe a clear experimental result comparing full-length BtuC, isolated TMH2, and the R→Q mutant (Figure 4b,e). The data support the conclusion that upstream positive charges delay integration. The CGMD simulation without membrane potential showing similar behavior (C63) provides additional support, though the mechanistic explanation (C64) remains somewhat speculative.

result: The low Nstart values for BtuC peaks V, X, and XI are attributed to early interactions between positively charged patches or short upstream hydrophobic segments with the membrane.
evaluation: Claims C59-C60 offer speculative explanations for shifted Nstart values. While C60 draws an analogy to GlpG peak III (which was experimentally validated), C59 lacks direct experimental support. The deletion construct (ΔTMH1-TMH4) provides some evidence for C59 but is not conclusive.

result: BtuC peaks VI and VII do not represent TMH6 integration but correspond to membrane insertion of a periplasmic re-entrant helix and cytoplasmic surface helix, respectively. Mutation of hydrophobic residues in the cytoplasmic surface helix reduces peak VII amplitude. The isolated TMH6 peaks between VI and VII at the expected location, indicating that flanking membrane-interacting segments strongly affect TMH6 integration.
evaluation: Claims C65-C68 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: force profiles of isolated TMH6, TMH5-6, and full-length BtuC (Figure 4b,g), plus mutagenesis of the cytoplasmic surface helix (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The data clearly demonstrate that flanking segments affect TMH6 integration.

result: Translocating nascent chains experience a distinct transition to a more hydrophobic environment at ~45 residues from the PTC, generating oscillating forces that vary with each TMH appearance at the translocon. TMHs stop generating force when their C-terminal ends reach ~45 residues from the PTC, regardless of orientation (Nout-Cin or Nin-Cout), at which point they are embedded in the membrane.
evaluation: Claims C69, C70, C73, and C78 synthesize observations across all three proteins studied (EmrE, GlpG, BtuC). The ~45 residue distance is consistently observed for both N-terminal (integration start) and C-terminal (integration end) positions across multiple TMHs with different orientations. This represents a major unifying finding of the study.

result: The results support the 'sliding' model of TMH integration, where Nout-Cin TMHs maintain continuous lipid contact while sliding across the membrane along the open lateral gate, while Nin-Cout TMHs first partition into the cytoplasmic membrane interface before inserting across the membrane. In both cases, TMHs are membrane-embedded when their C-terminal end is ~45 residues from the PTC. The translocon channel serves as a conduit for polar segments while hydrophobic segments remain in contact with lipid.
evaluation: Claims C74-C80, C86-C87 interpret the experimental data in the context of the sliding model. The observation that both Nout-Cin and Nin-Cout TMHs stop generating force at the same C-terminal distance from the PTC (C73, C78) provides strong support for this model. The interpretation is consistent with prior work (cites Cymer et al., 2014, 2015b) and the current data.

result: Force oscillations during membrane protein translation may have multiple effects, including ribosomal frameshifting and protein quality control.
evaluation: Claims C71-C72 are speculative, extrapolating from the observed force oscillations to potential functional consequences. While C71 cites a study on frameshifting (Harrington et al., 2020), the direct connection to the force oscillations observed here is not experimentally demonstrated in this manuscript.

result: High-resolution in vivo FPA reveals that: (1) an N-terminal cytoplasmic domain can fold in the ribosome exit tunnel before membrane integration; (2) force profiles match CGMD predictions to first approximation but reveal additional complexities including effects of charged residues and membrane-interacting segments (re-entrant loops, surface helices) on integration timing; (3) point mutations in upstream TMHs affect downstream TMH forces in a position-dependent manner, suggesting residue-specific inter-TMH interactions during integration; (4) nascent chains experience rapidly varying pulling forces during translation. This method can identify molecular interactions underlying cotranslational membrane protein biogenesis with single-residue precision.
evaluation: Claims C81-C92 summarize the major findings of the study. Each component is supported by experimental data: NTD folding (C31-C37), CGMD comparison (shown in all figures), effects of charged residues and flanking segments (EmrE E14 mutations, GlpG surface helix, BtuC Arg residues and re-entrant loops), position-dependent mutation effects (EmrE), and force oscillations (all force profiles). The claim about single-residue precision (C88) is supported by the single-residue resolution FPA performed for GlpG.

result: Prior work established that a model TMH generates a force profile peak when its N-terminal end is ~45 residues from the PTC, and FRET studies found the first TMH reaches the SecYEG translocon at 40-50 residues from the PTC.
evaluation: Claims C10-C11 cite prior work (Ismail et al., 2012; Mercier et al., 2020) establishing the ~45 residue distance. These are background claims that provide context for interpreting the current results.

result: Most integral membrane proteins are cotranslationally integrated via translocons (SecYEG, YidC, Sec61, EMC). While the energetics of TMH integration is reasonably well understood, the actual integration process is not well understood beyond general terms.
evaluation: Claims C93-C95 provide background context with appropriate citations (Rapoport et al., 2017; Chitwood et al., 2018; Hessa et al., 2007). These establish the knowledge gap that the study addresses.
